thread.title: UC researchers receive AAN Resident and Fellow Writing Award for case report
thread.title_full: UC researchers receive AAN Resident and Fellow Writing Award for case report

author: l. c. boyd
title: UC researchers receive AAN Resident and Fellow Writing Award for case report
text:
University of Cincinnati researchers were recognized on Apr. 14 as recipients of the 2026 American Academy of Neurology (AAN) Resident & Fellow Section Writing Award for a case report detailing the diagnostic journey of a young patient with early-onset parkinsonism.
The award highlights the importance of continuous re-evaluation in neurological diagnosis, especially when genetic origins are suspected but initial tests are inconclusive. The team’s article, first published on Feb. 27, 2025 in Neurology, described their process in identifying an early-onset genetic form of parkinsonism in a 24-year-old whose symptoms initially resembled dopa-responsive dystonia.
“The article walks through the clinical reasoning and diagnostic process over time, including longitudinal follow-up, systematic reassessment and genetic testing reanalysis,” said Luca Marsili, MD, corresponding author and assistant professor at UC’s Gardner Family Center for Parkinson’s Disease and Movement Disorders. “The key message is that in neurology, diagnosis is often not static but evolves over time, requiring continuous re-evaluation.”
Marsili also said that clinicians should continue to investigate all available data to reach a diagnosis when disease markers suggest a genetic cause—even if initial tests are negative. First author Nathaly Chinchihualpa, MD said: “This publication represents a sustained, collaborative effort to understand a challenging case over time. More broadly, it underscores that careful observation, diagnostic persistence and critical re-evaluation remain central to neurological practice.”
A follow-up report published by the team in February 2026 provided further insight into functional neurological symptoms emerging during advanced therapies for these conditions. “Altogether, this experience highlights the importance of clinical intuition, longitudinal follow-up and comprehensive evaluation,” Chinchihualpa said.
Marsili noted that recognition from AAN reflects growth within UC’s Movement Disorders Division—including being named an Ataxia Center of Excellence—and cited development of a dedicated neurogenetics clinic as part of ongoing efforts to improve care for patients with rare disorders. Chinchihualpa added: “This recognition from AAN is very meaningful… I am very grateful to the entire team for creating an environment where trainees can contribute meaningfully to complex clinical and research questions.”
Chinchihualpa credited her fellowship at UC with strengthening her approach to neurology under mentorship from Marsili and Alberto Espay; she continues training focused on neurogenetic disorders such as ataxia while managing research visits for genetic patients.
The research team thanked division codirectors Espay and Andrew Duker; counselor Kathleen Collins-Ruff; social workers Becca Gneuhs and Kaitlin Dejarnette; as well as participating patients.
